items.title: Application of Resonance and Standing Waves

source_refs.note: Application of Resonance and Standing Waves: a main subheading of 14.11 Sharpness of Resonance, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 39-40.

blocks.text: There are many applications of resonance in different devices that generate and use standing waves.
There is relationship between standing wave and resonance phenomenon which can be studied by some experimental examples such as Rubens tube, chaaladni plates and acoustic levitations.

A Rubens tube is a long tube which is an experimental apparatus used to explain the acoustic standing wave. It consists of a metal pipe with holes drilled a long top and sealed at both ends. One sealed end is attached to a small speaker or frequency generator while the other end is connected to supply of a flammable gas as shown in Fig (14.21). The pipe is filled with gas and gas leaks from holes and produce a resonant flame.

blocks.title: Interesting Information
blocks.text: A Rubens tube also known as standing wave flame tube or simply flame tube is a physics apparatus for demonstrating acoustic standing waves in a tube invented by a German physics Henrich Rubens in 1905.

blocks.alt: A gas cylinder feeds a long metal pipe with holes on top. The far end is closed by a membrane with a loudspeaker beyond it. A standing wave is drawn inside the pipe, and the flames above it are tall at the antinodes and short at the nodes.
blocks.caption: Figure 14.21: Rubens tube apparatus (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 14.21).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 14.21 shows tall flames only over the crests of the wave. Tall flames stand at every pressure antinode, crests and troughs alike, half a wavelength apart, as drawn above.

When sound waves of resonance frequency are produced by frequency generator, a standing wave is formed inside the tube. The standing wave creates points with oscillating (higher and lower) pressure within the tube. Less gas will escape from the holes in the tube where pressure is low, hence, the flame will be lower at these points. Large quantity of gas will escape from holes in the tube where pressure is high, hence, flame will be high at these points.
These low and high flame reveal the nodes and antinodes of standing waves inside the tube as shown in Fig. (14.21).
